name: Sulfasalazine
summary: Azo-prodrug split by colonic bacteria into 5-ASA (topical anti-inflammatory) and sulfapyridine (absorbed, and the source of most toxicity) — used in ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis.
mechanism: Colonic bacteria cleave the azo bond, releasing sulfapyridine (absorbed) and 5-ASA, which acts topically on the gut mucosa; also anti-inflammatory/DMARD effects in rheumatoid arthritis.

pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: ~10–15% absorbed intact; 5-ASA released locally by colonic bacteria

dosing.adult: IBD: 1 g 3–4 times daily; RA: titrate over weeks to 2–3 g daily in divided doses
dosing.maxDose: IBD acute: up to 4 g/day; RA: max 3 g/day
dosing.renalAdjustment: Use with caution in renal impairment; monitor

safety.pregnancy: Generally considered safe in IBD/RA; folate supplementation is essential
safety.lactation: Excreted in breast milk; caution in premature or jaundiced infants
warnings: Blood dyscrasias (agranulocytosis) — baseline and periodic CBC
Sulfa hypersensitivity — serious skin reactions possible
Reversible oligospermia — relevant in men planning children
safety.overdose: Nausea, vomiting; hemolysis in G6PD deficiency — supportive care

clinicalPearls: Turns urine, sweat, and tears orange-yellow — warn patients
Slow acetylators accumulate sulfapyridine and get more toxicity; folate supplementation is standard
good: Effective and inexpensive for both ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis
bad: Sulfa allergy, G6PD deficiency, renal/hepatic impairment; men planning a family (reversible oligospermia)

provenance.notes: Curated from standard pharmacology references. Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
